title: Equality and dictionary keys
sub: Equals without GetHashCode, and float compared with ==
cards/0/body:
Dictionary works like a cabinet with numbered drawers. To find a key, it takes two steps:

1. It asks the key for its drawer number (GetHashCode).
2. Inside that drawer, it compares keys for real (Equals).

If two "equal" keys give different numbers, the second one is searched for in the wrong drawer and never found.
cards/1/body: The ElementKey class overrides Equals but forgot GetHashCode. By default a class hash is tied to the specific object, not to its contents. Two different objects with identical fields get different numbers.
cards/1/deep: The contract: if a.Equals(b), the hashes must match. The reverse is not required (hash collisions are allowed). The compiler warns about this (CS0659), and that warning should not be silenced. For classes the default hash is built from object identity (RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode), and it stays the same even when the garbage collector moves the object. "Almost always" because two such hashes occasionally match by chance. A matching bucket is not enough: Dictionary first compares the stored full hash and only then calls Equals.
cards/2/q: What does this do to GetClashesFor in the service?
cards/2/options/0: The cache never hits: every call recomputes everything, and the cache grows
cards/2/options/1: An exception is thrown on first access
cards/2/options/2: The cache returns someone else's clashes
cards/2/explain: The caller creates a new key object every time, and ContainsKey does not find the "same" one. The query is recomputed and one more entry is added to the dictionary. Memory grows, speed is as if there were no cache.
cards/2/wrong/1: There is no exception: the dictionary just honestly says "not here".
cards/2/wrong/2: No foreign data appears, you only lose the cache hit.
cards/3/task: Find the problems with the dictionary key, the element identifier and the cache.
cards/3/bugs/0/why: Equal keys land in different dictionary drawers. ContainsKey cannot find them, the cache keeps growing, and every call recomputes everything.
cards/3/bugs/1/why: Once the hash depends on the fields (and it must), changing ElementId after insertion leaves the entry in its old drawer: it can be neither found nor removed. Public fields in a key invite exactly that.
cards/3/bugs/2/why: Elements from different models with the same number are indistinguishable: the a.Id < b.Id check skips their pair, so a clash between them is never found. And if Key is null, you get a NullReferenceException.
cards/3/bugs/3/why: ContainsKey, then the indexer: two lookups instead of one. On a hot path that is wasted work, fixed with TryGetValue.
cards/3/bugs/4/why: After clashes are added, removed or imported, the cached lists go stale, and the cache's internal mutable list is handed out to callers.
cards/4/q: Add the missing method so that equal keys produce the same drawer number.
cards/4/explain: HashCode.Combine mixes the field values into one hash. What matters is that the same fields take part as in Equals. In Unity, System.HashCode is available from 2021.2 (the .NET Standard 2.1 profile). On older versions, combine by hand: unchecked((ModelId?.GetHashCode() ?? 0) * 397 ^ ElementId).
cards/5/q: What happens if you change key.ElementId after dict[key] = value, and the hash is computed from that field?
cards/5/options/0: The entry stays in the old drawer and can no longer be found by the key
cards/5/options/1: The dictionary moves the entry to the new drawer itself
cards/5/options/2: An exception is thrown when the field changes
cards/5/explain: A dictionary computes the hash once, at insertion. It does not watch the key. That is why keys should be immutable: readonly fields, a record or a readonly struct.
cards/5/wrong/1: The dictionary does not know you changed the field and recomputes nothing.
cards/5/wrong/2: A plain field can be changed freely, nothing is checked.
cards/6/q: What is the right way to rewrite the double lookup?
cards/6/explain: TryGetValue searches once and returns the value right away. The second option searches twice and never stores anything in the cache. The third throws KeyNotFoundException when the key is missing.
cards/6/wrong/1: The lookup is still double, and Build's result is not saved anywhere.
cards/6/wrong/2: The indexer throws for a missing key, so ?? is never reached.
cards/7/explain: In C# the remainder takes the sign of the dividend. So Id % 8 for negative Ids gives a value from -7 to 0, and such elements never land in buckets 0...7. The fix: ((id % 8) + 8) % 8. Do not use Math.Abs: Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws OverflowException.
cards/7/wrong/1: That is how mathematicians do it (the remainder is never negative). In C#, the % operator works differently.
cards/7/wrong/2: The sign cannot vanish: the dividend is negative, so the remainder is too.
cards/8/body:
A computer stores float in binary, and many numbers (even a simple 0.1) cannot be written there exactly. Add 0.1 thirty times and you get 2.9999993, not 3. A == comparison will honestly say "not equal".

You need a tolerance: close enough means equal.
cards/8/code:
float h = 0f;
for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) h += 0.1f;   // 2.9999993
h == 3.0f;                       // false
Mathf.Approximately(h, 3.0f);    // true
Math.Abs(h - 3.0f) < 0.001f;     // tolerance in meters
cards/8/deep: Choose the tolerance for the problem at hand. Mathf.Approximately accepts a difference below 1e-6 of the larger magnitude (plus a tiny absolute floor of Mathf.Epsilon * 8). That is only a few steps of float precision: after a long chain of calculations the error can be larger, and near zero the check becomes almost exact. For heights in meters, an explicit tolerance is safer (for example, 1 mm). Also, NaN == NaN is false, so check for NaN separately.
cards/9/q: Which properties should a good dictionary key have? Pick all that apply.
cards/9/options/0: The fields that Equals and the hash depend on never change
cards/9/options/2: It implements IEquatable<T>, to avoid boxing
cards/9/options/3: The hash is computed from a Name field that the user can rename
cards/9/explain: Immutability and consistency between Equals and GetHashCode are required. IEquatable<T> removes the cast to object and boxing for structs. A hash over a mutable field breaks lookup.
cards/10/q: Match each problem with its consequence.
cards/10/pairs/0/1: The cache cannot find its own keys
cards/10/pairs/1/1: The entry is lost after an edit
cards/10/pairs/4/1: An element "on the level" is not recognized
cards/11/body: In modern .NET the shortest cure is readonly record struct ElementKey(string ModelId, int ElementId). The compiler generates Equals, GetHashCode, IEquatable<T> and the ==/!= operators, the properties become immutable, and the struct creates no garbage as a key.
cards/11/deep: A caveat for Unity: record needs C# 9, and record struct needs C# 10. Unity from 2021.2 through Unity 6 officially supports C# 9 (check your project's language version), so record struct is not available there, and a record class usually needs an IsExternalInit stub. The safe Unity option is by hand: readonly struct + IEquatable<ElementKey> + GetHashCode + ==/!= operators. If a struct implements neither IEquatable<T> nor an Equals override, the dictionary uses ValueType.Equals: boxing, plus reflection when there are reference fields. And ValueType.GetHashCode may then rely on the first field only, so every key of one model gets the same hash.
